raw_response:
Alright, let me think this through. I'm sitting here with my tea, planning the year.

---

*My reasoning, in my own voice:*

Forty years I've been on this land. Me and the old woman, just the two of us now — our son's in Shijiazhuang working construction, sends money when he can but he's got his own family to feed. Twenty mu is more than two old people should really manage, but the land is ours and we still have our strength, most days.

I can't read the papers the extension station puts up. Doesn't matter. I watch what Old Wang next door does — he's a good farmer, his wheat always stands tall — and I do about what he does. The agriculture station man came by last autumn and talked about some new method, but I've done it my way for forty years and I haven't starved yet. My way works.

I split the land like always. About 12 mu I do wheat then maize — two crops a year, that's what pays for the fertilizer and the electricity. The other 8 mu is cotton. Cotton is trouble, all that picking and spraying, but the price is decent and we've grown it here since I was a boy. My wife still has good hands for picking but we'll need to hire four or five women from the village for two weeks in autumn to get it all in.

**Wheat** — I plant around the Cold Dew period, early October, after the maize comes off. I use the seed I bought from the co-op last year, not the fancy new varieties. Before planting I put down one bag of compound fertilizer per mu — that's the blue-bag kind, 50 jin to a bag (I mean 50 kg, same thing). When the wheat starts jointing in spring, if it looks a bit yellow, I topdress with urea, maybe a third of a bag per mu. Some years I skip the topdress if money is tight. I irrigate three times — once before the ground freezes so the roots don't dry out, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling if it hasn't rained. That electricity bill adds up fast, the well is deep now. I spray herbicide once in spring for the weeds. I get about 400 kg per mu most years. Old Wang gets more but his son helps him.

**Maize** — The hardest week of the year. Wheat harvest is June, and the maize has to go in right behind it, within three or four days. I hire the combine for wheat, then hire a tractor with a planter for the maize — can't do it by hand at my age. I use hybrid seed, the kind in the yellow bag the shop sells. For maize I don't bother with base fertilizer much — I put some compound down with the seed, then one big topdress of urea when the plant is knee-high. Maybe one irrigation when it's tasseling if July is dry. I don't spray much for maize, sometimes a little something for borers. Yield maybe 400, 450 kg per mu.

**Cotton** — This is the worry crop. I plant mid-April after the ground warms up. Cotton wants more fertilizer than wheat, I put down compound at planting and then urea when it starts squaring. I irrigate twice usually, once after planting and once at bolling. Spraying is constant — aphids, bollworms, spider mites — I go through the field every week or two with the backpack sprayer. Two hundred fifty kg of lint per mu is a good year. When picking time comes in September my wife and I start, but there's no way we can pick 8 mu alone, so we hire help. That's the biggest cash outlay of the year.

If it's a good year we keep enough grain for ourselves and sell the rest. Cotton all goes to the buyer. I don't spend money I don't have — if fertilizer prices go up like last year, I use less, simple as that. Can't pour yuan into the ground when you haven't got them.
